1. Define the aggregate demand curve, explain why it
  slopes downward, and explain why it shifts
2. Define the aggregate supply curve, explain why it
  slopes upward, and explain why it shifts
3. Show how the aggregate demand curve and
  aggregate supply curve determine output and the
   inflation rate over the business cycle
4. Analyze how the economy adjusts to expansionary
  and recessionary gaps, and relate this to the
  concept of a self-correcting economy

• The (Keynesian) Aggregate Demand-Aggregate
  Supply model analyzes both inflation and output
   – Effective for analyzing the effects of macroeconomic
      policies
   – Applies to both the short run and the long run

• A primary objective of the Central Bank is to
  maintain a low and stable inflation rate
   – Inflation is likely to occur when Y > Y*
   – To control inflation, the Central Bank must keep Y from
     exceeding Y*
• When inflation increases,
   – The Central Bank increases the nominal interest rate
   – Real interest rates increase (contractionary policy)
   – Aggregate spending decreases via the multiplier effect

• A shift of the aggregate demand curve is
  called a change in aggregate demand
• At the given inflation rate, something
  causes output to rise (an increase in
  aggregate demand) or fall (a decrease in
  aggregate demand)
• Two main causes:
  – Demand shocks
  – Stabilization policy

  planned spending not caused by a change in
  output or a change in the inflation rate
   – Consumer confidence
   – Consumer wealth            𝜋𝜋

• People decide to save more:
  C falls, ADshifts left
• Stock market crash:
  C falls, ADshifts left
• Tax cut, household income rises:
  C rises, ADshifts right
• Firms become pessimistic about future demand:
  I falls, ADshifts left
• Technological progress creates many profitable
  business opportunities:
  I rises, ADshifts right
                                                                       12

• Government increases spending on police:
 G rises, ADshifts right
• Cuts in infrastructure spending on roads:
 G falls, ADshifts left
• A boom overseas increases foreign demand
  for our exports:
  NX rises, ADshifts right
• International speculators cause exchange
  rate to appreciate:
  NX falls, ADshifts left

• The Central Bank's monetary policy reaction function
   ties inflation to real interest rates
   – Suppose the Central Bank's targets are π1 and r1
            • MPRF is shown in the graph
•  Central Banks normally follows a stable MPRF
   – Central Bank can tighten
      or loosen monetary policy
            •  Shifts MPRF
   – Easing policy raises
      long-run inflation target
   – Tightening policy lowers
      long-run inflation target

•  Central Bank pursues fundamentally tighter monetary
   policy results in each level of inflation
  associated with a higher interest rate, r
• A upward shift of the MPRF

  π1

a. An increase in the price level

b. An increase in government purchases

c.  Higher state income taxes

d. Higher interest rates

e.  Faster income growth in other countries


                                                                         18

• The aggregate supply curve (AS) shows the
   relationship between the amount of output firms want
   to produce and the inflation rate
   – Holds all other factors constant
• The aggregate supply curve is upward sloping
   – An increase in aggregate demand will increase the
     willingness to supply and increase the inflation rate
•  In past chapters firms met demand at present prices
   – Holds in the very short run
   – Not possible to indefinitely hold inflation constant
    and increase output

                                                                         19

• Some firms have high menu costs
  – Costly to change price
• Some firms have very low menu costs
  – Internet retailers
  – Can increase price immediately in response to
    an increase in aggregate demand
• To produce more output, some firms need to
  eventually charge higher prices
  – Overworked resources
• Movement along the AS curve is related to inflation
   inertia and output gaps
                                                                        20

• Inflation inertia: inflation will remain
  relatively constant (“sticky”), as long as the
 economy is at potential output and there
  are no external shocks to the price level
• Two closely related factors that play an
  important role in determining the inflation
  rate
  – Inflation expectations
  – Long-term wage and price contracts

  realized inflation

• Long-term contracts reduce the cost of
  negotiations between buyers and sellers
   – Labor contracts may be multi-year agreements
   – Supply agreements, particularly for high cost inputs,
     extend over several years
• Long-term contracts build in wage and price
  increases that build in current expectations about
   inflation
•  In the absence of external shocks, inflation tends to
  be stable over time
   – Especially true in industrialized economies with low
      inflation

• An inflation shock is a sudden change in the
  normal behavior of inflation
   – unrelated to an output gap
• A sudden rise in the price of oil increases prices of
   – Gasoline, diesel fuel, jet fuel, heating oil
   – Goods made with oil (synthetic rubber, plastics, etc.)
   – Transportation of most goods
• OPEC reduced supplies in 1973; price of oil
  quadrupled
   – Food shortages occurred at the same time
   – Sharp increase in inflation in 1974
                                                                         30

• An adverse inflation shock shifts the
  aggregate supply curve to the left
  – Increases inflation at each output level
  – E.g.: Oil price increases in 1973; increases prices of
         • Gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, heating oil, electricity
         • Goods made with oil (synthetic rubber, plastics, …)
         • Transportation costs of most goods
• A favorable inflation shock shifts the
  aggregate supply curve to the right
  – Lower inflation at each output level
  – E.g.: Oil price decrease in 1986

• When output is above potential output, firms
  increase prices faster than the current expected
  rate of inflation
   – Causes expected inflation to increase
   – As inflation rises, the Fed increases interest rates
   – Consumption and planned investment spending
     decrease
   – Planned aggregate expenditures decrease
   – Output decreases
• This process continues until the economy reaches
  equilibrium at the potential level of output
   – Actual inflation is higher than initial level of inflation

•  In the long-run the economy tends to be self-correcting
   – Missing from the simple Keynesian model
   – Simple Keynesian model is only about the short-run;
    no price adjustments
• Given time, output gaps disappear without any changes
   in monetary or fiscal policy
• Whether stabilization policies are needed depends on
  the speed of the self-correction process
   – If the economy returns to potential output quickly,
      stabilization policies may be destabilizing
   – The greater the gap, the longer the adjustment period

                                                                          41

• A slow self-correcting mechanism
  – Fiscal and monetary policy can help stabilize the
    economy
• A fast self-correcting mechanism
  – Fiscal and monetary policy are not effective and
    may destabilize the economy
• The speed of correction will depend on
         • The use of long-term contracts
         • The efficiency and flexibility of labor markets
  – Fiscal and monetary policy are most useful when
     attempting to eliminate large output gaps
                                                                         42

• Large housing price bubble burst in July 2006
– 30% decline in housing prices over next 18 months
• Financial panic in the fall of 2008
– Difficult to borrow for households and firms
• Oil price shock
– Gas hit $4 per gallon in July 2008 (doubled from 2007)
      •  Although rising oil prices can result in a supply shock that causes the
     SRAS to shift to the left, it did not shift as far to the left during 2008 as
             it had from the increases in oil prices 30 years earlier because many
        firms had since switched to less oil-dependent production processes
– By January 2009, however, oil prices approximately
   returned to their January 2007 levels

• The basic AD-AS model we have seen so far
 adopts the assumption that the economy does
 not experience long-run growth
• We can develop a more general AD-AS
 model by dropping this assumption
• Now, takes into account that the economy is
 not static but dynamic, with potential real GDP
 that grows over time

                                                                         45

•  The LRAS curve shifts when there is a long-run change in a
   nation’s ability to produce output, or a change in potential level
   of real GDP
•  The factors that shift LRAS are the same factors that determine
  economic growth: resources, technology, institutions, etc.
• We can illustrate economic growth by using the LRAS curve

a. An increase in the price level

                                                                          47

• Changes in the dynamic model:
 – Potential real GDP increases continually,
    shifting the long-run aggregate supply curve to
    the right
 – During most years, the aggregate demand
    curve shifts to the right
 – Except during periods when workers and firms
    expect high rates of inflation, the short-run
    aggregate supply curve shifts to the right

• 1970s was a period of stagflation: a period of falling
  output and rising prices
• Adverse oil shocks and stagflation are policy challenges
   – Central Bank and Government can keep policies constant
         • Inflation will eventually decrease; unemployment
         eventually falls
         • However, economy has a prolonged high
       unemployment during adjustment
   –  If the government attacks unemployment with added
     government spending or the Central Bank loosens
     monetary policy
         • AD increases
         • Higher and higher inflation rates result
